job-title: Replace a kitchen countertop receptacle
job-setting: Occupied home. Homeowner says the outlet next to the sink is loose and sparks sometimes.

line 1: Danny
Alright, outlet by the sink is loose and the homeowner says it sparks sometimes. Easy swap. Heading to the panel in the garage.

line 2: Danny
Breaker's labeled kitchen. Flipping it off.

line 3: Danny
Kitchen lights just went out, so that's the right one. I'm not gonna bother with the tester, it's clearly dead. Back inside.

line 4: Danny
Cover plate's off. Backing out the two mounting screws and pulling the receptacle out of the box.

explain-panel: What's wrong, and why?
🎤 Talk
Submit
explain-input: He never tested that the circuit was dead with a meter before touching the wires
feedback-text: Good catch. Lights going out proves nothing about the receptacle. Countertop outlets are usually on separate small-appliance circuits, and panel labels are often wrong.

line 5: Danny
Grabbed a fifteen amp tamper-resistant duplex from the truck. It's next to the sink but a regular one's fine, the old one was regular too.

line 6: Danny
Checking the box while it's open. No cracks, and the wires have plenty of length to work with.

explain-panel: What's wrong, and why?
🎤 Talk
Submit
explain-input: Next to the sink it needs GFCI protection or someone could get a shock from the water

feedback-text: Good catch. Kitchen countertop receptacles, especially near a sink, need ground fault protection. Replacing like for like doesn't grandfather in a hazard. The fifteen amp rating is fine on a twenty amp kitchen circuit, the protection is what's missing.

line 7: Danny
Old one was wired with the push-in backstab holes. Doing the same on the new one, way faster than the screws.

line 8: Danny
Black to brass, white to silver, bare copper to the green ground screw.

explain-panel: What's wrong, and why?
🎤 Talk
Submit
explain-input: The wire has to wrap clockwise under the terminal screw or it works loose and heats up

feedback-text: Good catch. Push-in backstab connections loosen and heat up over time, and they're only listed for fourteen gauge wire. Kitchen counter circuits are usually twelve gauge. The sparking the homeowner reported was likely a failing backstab.

line 9: Danny
Folding the wires back in, mounting it, cover plate on.

line 10: Danny
Breaker back on. Plug-in tester shows two ambers, correct wiring. Done.
